questions.q: Per this lesson, why can't a smart contract make an HTTP request directly?
options: Consensus requires every node to compute the same result from the same input, and an HTTP call can return different answers to different nodes
HTTP requests are technically possible but disabled for security reasons the EVM team hasn't fixed yet
Smart contracts can make HTTP requests; this is a common misconception the lesson corrects
Gas costs for HTTP requests are too high to be economically viable
questions.explain: The lesson ties this directly to the determinism requirement from Lesson 14 — an HTTP call is non-deterministic, which breaks the agreement every validating node must reach.

questions.q: What specifically is "the oracle problem," as this lesson defines it?
options: The gap between needing external data on-chain and the fact that trusting one source to deliver it recreates the centralization smart contracts exist to avoid
The technical difficulty of writing Solidity code that compiles without errors
The fact that blockchains cannot store any data larger than 32 bytes
The problem of oracles being too expensive for small projects to afford
questions.explain: The lesson defines the oracle problem precisely as this gap: data must get on-chain, but a naive single-source oracle just renames the trust problem, not solves it.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a single trusted server pushing data on-chain doesn't actually solve the oracle problem?
options: Because it's a single point of failure and trust — if that server lies or goes offline, every dependent contract inherits the failure directly
Because a single server technically cannot submit transactions to a blockchain at all
Because it works perfectly and fully solves the problem; the lesson presents no issue with it
Because smart contracts are physically incapable of reading data from any external account
questions.explain: The lesson calls this out directly: one server is functionally identical to trusting one company's API, which is the exact centralization smart contracts exist to avoid.

questions.q: What three properties does this lesson say a real oracle fix needs?
options: Multiple independent nodes retrieving data separately, aggregation of their answers, and real economic cost for lying or failing to deliver
A single, highly trusted and well-funded company running the oracle exclusively
A requirement that all data come only from government-run APIs
Encryption of the data in transit, with no requirement for multiple sources
questions.explain: The lesson lists these three properties explicitly as mirroring what blockchain consensus itself relies on — independence, aggregation, and incentives.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what three real-world examples of contracts needing external data does it give?
options: A lending protocol needing an asset price, an insurance contract needing flight-delay status, and a prediction market needing an election result
A token contract needing to know its own total supply
An NFT contract needing to know how many NFTs it has minted so far
A wallet needing to know its own ETH balance
questions.explain: These are the three specific examples the lesson uses to show external data isn't an edge case but core to what makes smart contracts economically useful.
